summary: Describes known security threats against the Stream Control Transmission Protocol and how to counter them. It leans on techniques from the SCTP errata and issues memo, which were folded into RFC 4960. It is informational background for the protocol's security requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5062 lists the ways an attacker can misuse SCTP, the transport protocol that lets one device hold several IP addresses at once. For each attack it explains the mechanism and the countermeasure that the protocol specification now requires.

questions: how to protect sctp from attacks
what is address camping in sctp
subtitle: How an attacker can abuse SCTP's multiple addresses, and the checks the protocol now requires.

tldr.problem: SCTP lets one endpoint hold several IP addresses and send data over several paths. That flexibility creates security threats that a protocol with a single address does not have.
tldr.mechanism: The document works through each threat, describes the attack in detail, lists the conditions it needs, and names the countermeasure that the SCTP specification added for it.
tldr.outcome: The countermeasures are requirements in RFC 4960, which obsoleted RFC 2960. The document adds no rules of its own; it explains where each requirement came from.

today: RFC 5062 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It is background for RFC 4960, which turned the countermeasures it describes into requirements of the SCTP specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a multi-homed transport protocol, which means one endpoint can hold several IP addresses and send data over several paths. That flexibility creates security problems that a protocol with a single address does not have.

This document describes those threats and the ways to mitigate them, in particular the techniques taken from the SCTP Specification Errata and Issues memo (RFC 4460) and included in RFC 4960, which obsoleted RFC 2960. The authors credit the paper on potential SCTP security risks by Aura, Nikander and Camarillo, published at the IEEE Security and Privacy 2004 symposium.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP lets one device use several IP addresses, so traffic can keep flowing over another path when one fails. The same feature gives attackers new ways in. This document lists each attack and the fix the protocol specification now requires.

sections.title: Address Camping or Stealing
sections.content:
Address camping is a denial of service attack built on multi-homing. An attacker guesses the port number a client will use, opens an association with the server, and lists the victim's address, IP-C, in the initial INIT chunk as one of its own. The server accepts the association and believes the attacker holds both IP-A and IP-C.

When the real client then sends its own INIT, listing IP-C and IP-D, the server answers with an ABORT because an association already exists for that address. The client cannot connect until the server discovers that the attacker does not really hold IP-C.

The attack needs the attacker to set up the association first and to guess the victim's port number correctly. The existing HEARTBEAT mechanism eventually catches it, but that can take several seconds. RFC 4960 shortens the exposure. An address the endpoint did not know in advance enters a new UNCONFIRMED state, heartbeats to UNCONFIRMED addresses are sent at an accelerated rate of one per RTO, and each of those heartbeats carries a 64-bit random nonce that the reply must echo before the address may leave that state. Clients that do not need a fixed port should choose their port number at random.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who guesses a client's port number can open a connection to the server first and claim the client's address. The server then refuses the real client. The fix checks unclaimed addresses with a secret random number, and sends those checks more often than usual.

sections.title: Association Hijacking
sections.content:
Association hijacking means one user takes over a session created by another endpoint. The first variant needs an address that was recently in use by an SCTP endpoint, for example an address reassigned by DHCP to a migrant host. If the ASCONF chunk that tells the peer about the new address is lost, the peer still believes the old owner holds the association. The new owner of the address can see a DATA chunk, send an INIT, and receive an INIT-ACK whose cookie holds the tie-tags. Those tags let it add its own addresses to the association and take it over.

RFC 4960 requires that the tie-tags in the state cookie are not the real tags: a pair of 32-bit nonces stands in for them, so the real tags never leave the endpoint. Using the dynamic address reconfiguration extension, RFC 5061, also requires the authentication mechanism of RFC 4895, and an endpoint-pair shared key stops an attacker who merely captured the setup exchange from taking the association over.

The second variant needs no weakness in the protocol at all. An attacker who can send from and receive to the victim's address performs a full four-way handshake using the same addresses and port numbers, and the peer treats it as a restart. If the upper layer ignores the restart notification, the attacker has the association. The countermeasure is for the application to process the restart notifications described in section 10 of the SCTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attacks let the new owner of an IP address take over someone else's connection. One is stopped by keeping the real connection tags inside the endpoint and putting random numbers in their place in the cookie. The other is stopped only by the application noticing that the connection restarted.

sections.title: Bombing Attacks
sections.content:
A bombing attack makes an endpoint send many packets, or a large reply, to an innocent third party, the victim, in response to one packet from the attacker. Five variants are described.

  • In the first, the attacker lists the victim's address in its INIT, requests a large data transfer, and then stops acknowledging the data. The server retransmits to the alternate address, which is the victim's. Proper handling of ICMP messages fails the association at the first retransmission, and RFC 4960 forbids sending DATA chunks to any address that is not CONFIRMED. An implementation should also abort the association when a SACK acknowledges a TSN that was never sent, which makes guessing transmission sequence numbers hard.
  • In the second, the attacker sends an INIT listing several victim addresses and optionally asks for a long cookie lifetime. Each time it returns the stored cookie, the endpoint answers with up to HB.Max.Burst heartbeats to the victim. The counters are a limit on cookie lifetimes, a limit on the HB.Max.Burst value, and small heartbeats.
  • The third variant exploits a response that needs several chunks. If the endpoint does not bundle chunks when sending, it answers with one packet per chunk, using the victim's address as the source. Verifying the path before sending any chunk other than a path-verification heartbeat, and bundling on the sending side, prevent it.
  • The fourth variant is byte amplification. A packet sent from the victim's address carrying an INIT makes the server reply with an INIT-ACK that is most likely larger than the request. The only countermeasure is to keep the generated INIT-ACK as small as possible, and the padding parameter of RFC 4820 is named as a possible way to avoid it.
  • The fifth variant uses a difference in path maximum transmission unit. The attacker sends a packet that makes the endpoint answer with several chunks. If the path towards the attacker has a smaller MTU than the path towards the victim, the responding endpoint may need more than one packet to carry all the chunks. The difference can be extreme if the attacker sends malicious ICMP packets to influence path MTU discovery. The fix is to verify the path first and to drop the chunks that do not fit instead of sending extra packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Five variations of one trick: make a server send a flood of packets, or a large reply, to somebody else. The counters are to check the path before sending, to bundle chunks together, to limit heartbeats and cookie lifetimes, to keep the first reply small, and to refuse to send data to an address that has not been confirmed.

sections.title: Association Redirection
sections.content:
Association redirection lets an attacker set up an association to a different endpoint than the one intended. The attacker sends an INIT from port X towards port Y. When the INIT-ACK comes back, it sends the COOKIE-ECHO chunk with a different source or destination port in the SCTP common header, X+1 or Y+1, and the association may then be set up with the modified ports.

The attack works only when an implementation fails to store and verify the ports inside the COOKIE structure. The countermeasure is to include both the source and destination ports in the cookie, and to silently discard a returned COOKIE whose ports do not match the stored ones.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can change the port numbers in the setup reply so that the connection ends up on the wrong endpoint. The fix is to store the real port numbers in the cookie the server sends, and check them when the cookie comes back.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Countermeasure Summary
sections.content: The document says it has no additional security considerations of its own, because it is about security. What it provides is a summary of the countermeasures now in the SCTP specification: the UNCONFIRMED address state with nonce-protected heartbeats, tie-tags replaced by nonces in the state cookie, authenticated chunks required for dynamic address reconfiguration, port numbers stored and checked inside the cookie, limits on heartbeats and cookie lifetimes, bundling on the sending side, path verification before sending other chunks, and the rule that no DATA chunk is sent to an address that is not CONFIRMED.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no rules of its own. It collects the countermeasures the SCTP specification now requires, so that implementers and reviewers can see which attack each one answers.

messages.label: INIT listing IP-A and IP-C
messages.note: The attacker claims the victim's address IP-C.

messages.label: INIT-ACK
messages.note: The server believes the attacker holds both addresses.

messages.label: ABORT
messages.note: An association already exists for IP-C, so the client is refused.

messages.label: HEARTBEAT with 64-bit nonce
messages.note: The nonce must come back echoed before IP-C leaves the UNCONFIRMED state.

viz.caption: ATTACK AND THE COUNTERMEASURE THE SPECIFICATION ADDED

items.title: Address camping
items.text: UNCONFIRMED state, heartbeats every RTO, 64-bit nonce in each heartbeat.

items.title: Association hijacking
items.text: Tie-tags replaced by a pair of 32-bit nonces; authenticated chunks required.

items.title: Bombing attack 1
items.text: No DATA chunk to an address that is not CONFIRMED; handle ICMP; abort on a SACK for an unsent TSN.

items.title: Bombing attack 2
items.text: Limit cookie lifetimes and the HB.Max.Burst value; keep heartbeats small.

items.title: Bombing attacks 3 and 5
items.text: Verify the path before sending; bundle chunks; drop chunks that do not fit.

items.title: Bombing attack 4
items.text: Keep the generated INIT-ACK as small as possible.

items.title: Association redirection
items.text: Store the source and destination ports in the cookie and discard a mismatch.
